newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan tourist mecca draws political heavyweights.
newsitem.headline: Japan tourist mecca draws political heavyweights.

text.p: In Japan's ancient seaside capital of Kamakura, whose Great Buddha and good surfing attract millions of visitors each year, vans full of heavyweight politicians with megaphones at full blast vied with tour buses on narrow, bamboo-lined roads on Thursday.

"I'm Morihiro Hosokawa ... and Kamakura is special to me because I went to elementary and middle school here," said the popular former prime minister, the latest in a series of Tokyo bigshots to make the one-hour trip from Tokyo.

Kamakura's 140,000 voters are also vital to the opposition Shinshinto (New Frontier Party), of which Hosokawa is a top official, in its October 20 election fight against the Liberal Democratic Party and other groups under Japan's brave new world of the first-past-the-post electoral system.
"There can be only one winner -- and no one feels very safe, so every vote counts," said Junichiro Koizumi, a top LDP figure campaigning on behalf of Tadayoshi Iijima.
Iijima and Shinshinto's Keiichiro Asao are seen as the top contenders.

Best known for the Buddhist temples and samurai graves that remain from its 12th century political heyday, thickly-forested Kamakura represents many suburban centres that have gained political clout at the expense of rural areas under a drastic overhaul of the electoral system in 1994.

"Kamakura has a garden image, but it is a microcosm of Japan, with serious concerns about the sluggish economy and unemployment, the welfare costs of a rapidly aging society and fiscal problems," said Shinichiro Toyama, secretary general of the Kamakura Chamber of Commerce and Industry.
The new electoral system was designed to force politicians to address such concerns, replacing traditional pork barrel electioneering with party politics and policy debate.

But voters say they are confused by the system, which features 300 single-seat constituencies and 200 decided by proportional representation in 11 regional blocs. A recent poll found 43 percent of voters did not know their new district.

Campaign officials for the six Kamakura candidates -- all new faces in a new district -- say they spend most of their time selling their candidates' names, a job made easier with the help of former prime ministers and other national figures.

"The new system was supposed to usher in the era of party politics, but so far it remains the same as before -- peddling the candidate's name along the back alleys and footpaths," said a campaign official of the new Democratic Party.

Shinshinto's Hosokawa was to be followed on Thursday by Yukio Hatoyama, who last month formed the Democratic Party to win over undecided voters -- the 50 percent of the electorate who may decide the election.
Both Shinshinto and the Democrats are fighting on the same basic message -- streamlining the bureacracy and cutting red tape, tasks they say the LDP has shown it has no stomach for.
"Government is a sick patient. It is corpulent, it is dizzy, and its pulse is slowing," said Hosokawa. "Shinshinto wil put the patient on a strict diet."
LDP candidate Iijima said his party would restore stability to Japanese politics and regain Japan's standing in the world after years of revolving door governments.

"U.S. President Clinton has met five prime ministers in four years, and the late French President MItterand saw 10 in 13 years," Iijima told a crowd. "The world must be wondering who exactly is in charge here."
